prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, based on magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms, which brought atomic time and frequency measurement to the 1e-18 level.

statement.case_for: I keep B024 as my preferred single part, but I have changed how I would defend it after the first-round exchange. The achievement is an invention with a physical idea of its own: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the light shift while Lamb-Dicke confinement removes Doppler and recoil effects, for very many neutral atoms interrogated at once. Ye's strontium clocks and the intercomparisons between independent laboratories showed what that buys, uncertainty and stability near 1e-18, roughly two orders of magnitude beyond the caesium standard. That performance is reproduced at many institutes, so the claim is about delivered capability and not a bet on future results. The credited pair maps onto invention and realisation with no third name forced out, and no member has argued that B024 is scientifically premature or unconfirmed. I now accept Lindroth's correction that the citation should rest on invention and realisation, with the geodesy, constant-variation and dark-matter work described as what the capability makes possible and not as discoveries already made. That is a narrower claim than my round-1 wording, and it is the one the evidence supports.
statement.case_against: The overlap with the 2005 and 2012 metrology prizes is a real worry for a committee that wants a new subject, and I cannot show that every member will accept my distinction between combs, single-ion control and many-atom magic-wavelength trapping. B024 also has less breadth of opening support than B044, and I cannot rule out that my weighting of precision measurement reflects my own background in laser spectroscopy and a documented stay in John Hall's laboratory. The new-physics payoff and the redefinition of the second are still prospective, and Lindroth is right that the constant and dark-matter tests have so far set limits. On the other side, B044 is a strong, mature candidate whose attribution gap (Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang for HgTe/CdTe, and the three-dimensional work) is a limit of a three-name set and not a flaw in the science. If the committee decides that discovery of a new phase of matter outweighs a clean credit, I could accept B044 with a citation restricted to the prediction and the HgTe quantum-well discovery. I do not regard the missing names as disqualifying; I regard a clean two-name credit as an advantage that I weigh above breadth of support.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B024 as the sole part but asks that the citation stress invention and realisation, because the tests of constants and dark matter have so far only set limits, and she notes that Ye's platform spread and the Yb, Hg and Al+ clock communities could prompt questions about omissions.
responses.response: I move toward you on both points. The citation I now propose names the magic-wavelength lattice and the realisation at 1e-18, and drops any implication that new physics has already been found. On omissions, I think the two-name credit holds: the claim is the lattice idea (Katori) and its realisation as an accuracy and stability benchmark (Ye), and the early Yb and Hg lattice work and the Al+ ion clocks were demonstrations of or comparisons with that idea, not alternative inventions of it. I would still say in the committee that the credit is the lattice clock and not the whole field of optical clocks, so the Ludlow and Al+ communities have a clear answer to why the prize is not broader.

responses.point: Pearce supports B024 as one part of a two-part prize with B019, asks that the citation emphasise the magic-wavelength lattice rather than a record accuracy figure, and proposes Halzen alone for IceCube.
responses.response: I accept the wording request; the magic-wavelength lattice is now the named idea in the citation, with the 1e-18 level as the demonstration. I do not accept the pairing. The IceCube science is well established and I have no doubt about the diffuse flux, but a sole credit to Halzen for a detector built and operated by a large collaboration would hide the AMANDA and IceCube builders, and the protocol does not let us add names. Pairing it with B024 would make a strong two-name part carry a part I cannot defend publicly. I would rather award B024 on its own now and see neutrino astronomy recognised later with a credit set that fits it.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B044 and ranks B024 low because it continues a line recognised in 2005 and 2012 and because the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, but she keeps B024 as an alternative and says the Kane-Mele core could be kept intact in the citation.
responses.response: Your point that the quantised edge conductance in HgTe wells is accessible experimental evidence is fair, and it is why B044 is my first alternative. On the continuation worry, I still read the 2005 prize as the frequency ruler and the 2012 prize as control of single ions; neither covers neutral atoms trapped in a lattice at the magic wavelength, which is the step that changes the stability regime. On the redefinition, independent laboratories already agree at the 1e-18 level, so the timing of an administrative decision does not change the scientific evidence. I do concede that your Kane-Mele-core wording is a defensible way to handle the attribution gap if the committee prefers B044.

responses.point: Eriksson, who moved to B044, argues that cleanness of credit is not the same as breadth of scientific consequence and that the topological classification has reshaped a whole subfield, and he proposes a citation tied to the prediction and its discovery in HgTe quantum wells.
responses.response: I agree that breadth of consequence is a legitimate criterion and that B044 scores very well on it, and I am glad your proposed wording avoids claiming the three-dimensional work. Where I differ is that a clock's consequence is broad in a different way: a standard that is two orders of magnitude better feeds into geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and time distribution, but these are not yet visible as a subfield the way topological materials are. So we weigh a visible subfield against a capability whose consequences are still arriving. Because the credit for B044 depends on a wording compromise and the credit for B024 does not, I still place B024 first, but I regard the difference as one of judgement and not of evidence.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts magic-wavelength many-atom lattice trapping as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, or reads B024 as a continuation of that lineage.
Whether the committee weights clean attribution (B024) above broader opening support and visible subfield impact (B044), which is a judgement about the committee's criteria and not a scientific fact.
Whether the redefinition of the second will come before or after a prize, and how that should be mentioned in a citation that stresses invention and realisation.
I rely on memory for priority details between Katori's proposal and parallel lattice-clock ideas, and I have not verified them independently.
statement.conflict_note: No change from round 1. I have no documented personal or institutional tie to Katori or Ye. I disclose again that my research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder is documented, and that Hall is a laureate in a field adjacent to precision measurement; this is a field and network connection, not a tie to the candidates. I also work in laser spectroscopy and quantum optics, which is close in subject to optical clocks. My Lund colleagues (Rippe, Walther, Kinos), WACQT and Deep Light Vision do not relate to B024, B044 or B036. I note the chair's question on recording flags: I am content for the Boulder stay to be recorded, and I do not think it changes the weight of my position on B024. The recusal question on B042 concerns Johansson, not me.
